query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating an in‐situ laser remelting step immediately after each deposited layer during SLM of high-entropy alloys will refine the microstructure, reduce residual defects, and thereby improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity compared to conventional SLM processing.
generation.material_initial_state: SLM‐fabricated HEA components (e.g., CoCrFeNiMn) produced with standard process parameters that exhibit residual porosity, keyhole defects, microcracks, and dimensional distortions due to rapid solidification and steep thermal gradients.
generation.intervention: Incorporate an in‐situ laser remelting pass over each freshly deposited layer, using optimized laser power and scanning speed to re‐melt the surface without degrading the overall part geometry.
generation.conditions: Process in an inert atmosphere with controlled substrate pre-heating as needed; use laser parameters tuned to avoid overheating or keyholing; applicable to SLM‐fabricated HEA parts processed under typical industrial additive manufacturing settings.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined melt pool boundaries and homogenized microstructure with reduced porosity and residual stress, leading to more uniform layer bonding and fewer microcracks.
generation.mechanism: The extra laser remelting pass redistributes heat more uniformly across each layer, diminishing sharp thermal gradients and associated residual stresses. This controlled re-melting facilitates grain refinement and the healing of intra-layer defects (e.g., pores and microcracks), which in turn limits the accumulation of dimensional inaccuracies and improves mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Parts produced with the in‐situ remelting treatment will exhibit improved dimensional accuracy (less warping and geometric deviation) and enhanced mechanical properties (higher tensile strength, improved ductility, and fatigue resistance) relative to parts made by conventional SLM.
generation.baseline: Conventional SLM-processed HEA parts commonly show defects such as porosity, microcracking, and dimensional distortions due to rapid cooling and inherent thermal gradients.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness may be limited if the alloy has an extremely high melting point or if the remelting parameters are not precisely controlled; excessive remelting could cause overheating, coarsening, or even new defect formation. The intervention’s benefits might also diminish in systems where the as-deposited microstructure is already near-optimal.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvements in mechanical properties and dimensional precision is uncertain. This hypothesis extends the benefits observed from laser remelting in Al0.65CoCrFeNi HEA (PMC9919236) and thermal management strategies from DED crack-mitigating studies (PMC12348559) to a broader class of SLM-fabricated HEAs.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of identical HEA components (e.g., CoCrFeNiMn): one set using standard SLM and the other using the in-situ laser remelting step immediately after each layer. Use 3D scanning to assess dimensional accuracy and perform microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM, EBSD) plus tensile and fatigue testing to compare mechanical properties.
measurements: 3D dimensional and geometric deviation measurements using high-resolution scanning
Defect density evaluation via scanning electron microscopy and X-ray tomography
Mechanical performance (tensile strength, ductility, fatigue life) through standardized tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the in-situ remelted parts do not display statistically significant improvements in dimensional fidelity and mechanical properties – or if defect density is not reduced relative to the conventional SLM parts – then the hypothesis is considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The conventional manufacturing of refractory complex concentrated alloys (RCCAs) for high-temperature applications is complicated, particularly when material costs and high melting points of the materials processed are considered. Additive manufacturing (AM) could provide an effective alternative. However, the extreme temperatures involved represent significant challenges for manufacturing defect-free alloys using this approach. To address this issue, we investigated the preparation of a CrNbTiZr quaternary complex concentrated alloy from an equimolar blend of elemental powders using commercially available powder-blown L-DED technology. Initially, the alloys exhibited some defects owing to the internal stress caused by the temperature gradients. This was subsequently resolved by optimizing the deposition strategy. SEM, XRD and EDS were used to analyze the alloy in the as-deposited condition, revealing a BCC phase and a secondary Laves phase. Furthermore, Vickers hardness testing demonstrated a correlation between the hardness and the volume fraction of the Laves phase. The laser remelting technique was applied to the surface modification of the Al0.65CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) to further advance its mechanical potential. The microstructure of the remelted layer was refined from coarse dendritic to submicron-scale basket weave compared with the as-cast substrate, resulting in a 1.8-time increase in Vickers microhardness. The nanoindentation tests indicated that the nanohardness of the remelted layer was higher than that of each phase in the substrate. Meanwhile, the remelted layer retained considerable plasticity, as evidenced by its high Wp/Wt ratio (0.763) and strain hardening exponent (0.302). Additionally, adhesive wear prevailed on the substrate, while only abrasive wear features were observed on the remelted layer. Accordingly, the average friction coefficient and the wear rate of the remelted layer were minimized by 23% and 80%, respectively, compared with the substrate. Our findings explored an industrialized method to enhance the surface properties of the Al0.65CoCrFeNi HEA and also provided some helpful references for its laser additive manufacturing.
